canberra.title: ANU governance intentions locked in as efforts continue to fill key leadership roles
canberra.snippet: The Australian National University’s governance will be “transparent, inclusive and fiscally responsible” from here on ...
canberra.content:
ANU interim Vice-Chancellor Professor Rebekah Brown. Photo: Claire Fenwicke.

The Australian National University’s governance will be “transparent, inclusive and fiscally responsible” from here on out, its latest strategy has promised.

The ANU by 2030 strategy stated the way it operated would be a strength, “competent, straightforward”, and would involve “meaningful” staff and student engagement.

“It will deliver community safety; academic freedom; disciplined risk management; and contestable resource allocation,” it stated.

“We recognise that we have not always met these standards. Rebuilding trust requires us to be open about where we have fallen short and disciplined in how we improve.

“Institutional decisions will be communicated clearly, with the rationale, evidence and risks openly explained.”

It marks a line in the sand for the past few tumultuous years.

The fallout from the disastrous and unjustified Renew ANU program – which saw hundreds of staff made redundant, severe psychosocial impacts on staff, and massive changes in the university’s structure and culture – culminated in both Vice-Chancellor Genevieve Bell and Chancellor Julie Bishop stepping down.

It followed unprecedented amounts of community and political pressure.

Ms Bishop’s departure led to mass resignations from the ANU Council, with a majority of the external positions still to be filled.

Along with seeking a new Chancellor (through an independent selection process following intervention by the sector regulator), ANU is also advertising for new heads of the finance and audit and risk committees.

Interim Vice-Chancellor Professor Rebekah Brown said the release of the strategy was about strengthening ANU’s foundations, resilience and setting its trajectory ahead of these appointments.

“It’s at a time where our incoming Chancellor and our next forthcoming substantive Vice-Chancellor will have a real role in shaping how we realise the intent of our strategy,” she said.

“The council that we have at the moment, albeit a much smaller one … are incredibly hardworking, incredibly diligent. [It] is meeting multiple times per week, has endorsed this strategy and the commitments in this strategy.”

The strategy went through two draft versions, more than 100 forums, an online feedback portal and feedback from more than 1000 staff, students and alums before being released.

It doesn’t contain any concrete numbers or commitments; rather, it provides the overall direction ANU wanted to go.

Ms Brown said more detail was underway.

“The next stage of our work is to develop our implementation plan and in some ways that’s even harder work,” she said.

“In our implementation plan we’ll be setting out our key responsibilities, our key activities, our key targets, and it’s a really important moment for us because we’re in transition in our governance, and so it’s a very deliberate strategy … being built by our community, for our community.”

“The core message is that we’re actually a fantastic institution. We deliver on our promise of great research, great education, and really important convening for the nation. We contribute to sovereign national capability building.

“The strategy is about investing in that, reinforcing that [in] our fundamental principles, but looking at how we do that for a new age, for the next 80 years.”

Ms Brown hoped a new chancellor would be announced “sooner rather than later”.

“We need a new chancellor, we need the full complement of our new council, and then that council will decide, together with the community, the sort of leadership that’s needed going forward,” she said.

A permanent Vice-Chancellor position is yet to be advertised.

One newer section of the strategy touches on the use of artificial intelligence.

Ms Brown said it wasn’t about replacing human jobs but to accept that, like all other institutions across the world, AI was becoming part of life.

“We need to make sure that we’re using it well and we’re using it meaningfully and we’re really deliberate in how we use it, and it’s really to support our people so that we can spend our time being really strategic with our efforts,” she said.

“We’re in an AI-fluent world now, and so that’s something that we embrace at ANU, and we’ll be taking very deliberate steps to make sure that our graduates, in the future, are AI-fluent.”

Sustainable student numbers are identified as key in the strategy, but there are still no set targets.

As the university celebrates its 80th anniversary, Ms Brown said the budget would be in deficit this year, but behind-the-scenes work is underway to boost revenue.

More details are expected in the coming weeks, but right now she wanted the ANU community to take stock of what it had achieved.

“[This] is a day for our community, it’s a day for us to celebrate, it’s a day to put the last two years, some of that, behind us for us to look forward,” Ms Brown said.

canberra.title: Agreement signed on possible acquisition of Australian-designed radars by UK
canberra.snippet: Australia and the UK have signed an agreement to progress the possible acquisition of Australian-designed radar systems by the UK Ministr...
canberra.content:
CEA Technologies CEO Alan Clements, Interim UK National Armaments Director Nadine Williams, Chair of CEA Technologies Joycelyn Morton, Minister for Defence Industry Pat Conroy, UK Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry Luke Pollard, UK Director General International National Armaments Director Group Avril Joliffre, Australia QinetiQ CEO Corry Neale, Head of Air Defence and Space Systems Division Air Vice-Marshal Martin Nussio, and CEA Engineering Development Manager Craig Hill at the signing on 12 August. Photo: QinetiQ.

Australia and the UK have signed an agreement to progress the possible acquisition of Australian-designed radar systems by the UK Ministry of Defence (MoD), with reports indicating a possible future $10 billion contract with the UK could be Australia’s largest-ever defence sale.

The advanced electronically scanned array (AESA) radar systems are designed and built by Canberra-based majority Government-owned CEA Technologies, and the agreement includes British company QinetiQ, which will play a role in the integration, testing and assurance of the arrays into the UK defence system.

The joint statement signed between Defence, CEA, QinetiQ and the UK MoD on 12 August was witnessed by Defence Industry Minister Pat Conroy, and visiting UK Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry Luke Pollard.

The agreement recognises the strategic importance of collaboration between both nations’ defence departments and defence industries, and commits Australia and the UK to working closely together to implement the AESA radar initiatives announced in June’s Australia-UK Ministerial Consultations (AUKMIN) summit.

The agreement aligns with the AUKUS Pillar 2 construct which seeks to deepen cooperation between Australia, the UK, and US on a number of advanced technologies including cyber, hypersonics, undersea technologies, uncrewed systems, quantum computing, and electronic warfare.

In Australian Defence Force service, CEA arrays are used for search and air defence on the navy’s ANZAC-class frigates, on the amphibious vessel HMAS Choules, as key sensors for the Army’s new NASAMS short-range air defence and HIMARS long-range fires systems, and as threat emulators on the Air Force’s electronic warfare training range in support of the EA-18G Growler electronic attack aircraft.

CEA is also developing the main sensor for the Navy’s new Hunter-class frigates from 2032.

Minister Pollard said Australia and the UK were deepening their industrial cooperation with Australia on cutting-edge radar technologies.

“By bringing QinetiQ’s expertise together with CEA’s world-class radar technology, we can strengthen the warfighting readiness of both our nations while backing jobs and growth on both sides of the world,” he said.

Group CEO of QinetiQ, Steve Wadey added, “QinetiQ’s unique expertise positions us as a strategic and trusted partner to the UK Ministry of Defence and its allies.

“Current conflicts remind us of the importance of air defences, which are increasingly under pressure, and QinetiQ is proud to play a key role in bringing this vital technology to the UK.”

The new CEO of CEA Technologies Alan Clements said the signing was an important milestone for CEA and the Australian and UK defence industries.

“It reflects the confidence both governments have in CEA’s world-leading radar technology and the important role industry partnerships play in strengthening sovereign capability.”

Original Article published by Andrew McLaughlin on PS News.

canberra.title: WATCH: Teen found hiding in rubbish bin after allegedly driving stolen vehicle
canberra.snippet: Police have released footage of officers popping open a rubbish bin to find a teenage boy wanted for allegedly driving a stolen car throu...
canberra.content:
Police found the 15-year-old boy hiding in a rubbish bin on 14 August 2026. Photo: ACT Policing.

Police have released footage of officers popping open a rubbish bin to find a teenage boy wanted for allegedly driving a stolen car through Canberra.

An ACT Policing spokesperson alleged a Toyota LandCruiser was stolen from Duffy on either Tuesday or Wednesday (11-12 August) after intruders entered a home and took the keys.

On Thursday afternoon, officers spotted the LandCruiser in Greenway. It was allegedly seen speeding and evading police.

The police spokesperson said it was then found in Kambah, but alleged its driver took off again when officers approached.

Shortly afterwards, a member of the public told police the car had been abandoned in Waramanga and two youths had been seen running from the area.

Officers began to search the area before they used body-worn cameras to film themselves finding a 15-year-old boy hiding in a residential rubbish bin outside a home in Stirling.

He was handcuffed before police helped him out of the bin.

The teenager was scheduled to face the ACT Childrens Court on Friday (14 August) charged with driving a motor vehicle without consent and driving without a licence.

canberra.title: Big tech now has to make deals with even more local news outlets
canberra.snippet: Google, Meta and other giant tech companies that share Australian-produced news on their platforms will soon have to strike deals with ev...
canberra.content:
Global social media giants will have to make deals with eight Australian news firms to avoid additional taxes. Photo: hocus-focus.

Google, Meta and other giant tech companies that share Australian-produced news on their platforms will soon have to strike deals with even more local media firms to avoid an extra 2.5 per cent tax.

Revised legislation aimed at protecting Australian journalism and news media has been introduced to Federal Parliament, following talks between Anthony Albanese and Angus Taylor.

The Prime Minister and Opposition Leader met to discuss last-minute changes to Labor’s News Bargaining Incentive and the News Journalism Payments bills, to reach agreement for them to pass both Houses.

The biggest change to come from those talks and wider consultation is that the big tech companies will have to make deals with eight local media outlets, up from six stipulated in the previous draft and four in an even earlier draft.

The bills address a limitation in the long-standing News Media Bargaining Code that has allowed digital platforms to avoid paying for news content by removing news from their service.

The legislation now also reinstates the per-deal cap of 25 per cent of the total levy, ensuring that more appropriate offsets are available to Australian media organisations of all sizes, more closely reflecting their reach and significance in the market.

This rule limits any single commercial agreement between a tech platform and a news outlet from offsetting more than a quarter of the platform’s total levy liability.

The year the base rate is calculated is also being brought forward by two years, rather than three, to better reflect the actual state of deals in the Australian market in recent years.

And 5 per cent of the incentive’s funds will be directed to the Australian Associated Press (AAP) in recognition of its role in supporting public-interest journalism and news organisations across Australia.

Another special allocation of 5 per cent of revenue raised will go into a grants scheme to help small publishers and start-ups in local communities.

In introducing the bills to the House of Representatives on Thursday (13 August), Communications Minister Anika Wells said the legislation aimed to encourage commercial deals between digital platforms and news publishers.

“Journalism matters. It matters to our democracy, to the health and cohesion of our communities, and to Australians who rely on trusted reporting to understand what is happening locally, nationally and around the world,” she said.

“Quality journalism is costly to produce, and the economics of producing news have changed.”

The minister said the Federal Government was “delivering for journalists” to ensure they get their fair share from digital platforms that benefit from Australian news.

“A diverse, strong and sustainable media sector is an essential part of a robust democracy,” Ms Wells said.

“People access news in different ways and from different sources, which is why we made changes to the distribution scheme to better support smaller and diverse media organisations.”

Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino was earlier doing the media rounds to spruik the revised legislation.

He described it as a “significant day for the future of Australian journalism” and said the legislation delivers a “very strong incentive” for big tech to enter into agreements with regional media, culturally diverse media and LGBTQI media in Australia.

“We want to see deals between digital platforms and a diverse range of media organisations to ensure fair recompense for the use of content,” he said.

“We also want to ensure the media sector is strengthened from large companies to small ones, recognising the significant benefits strong journalism brings to communities across the nation.”

Mr Mulino said Australia’s media companies would receive more money under the revised legislation.

“We’re changing the reference year to one year forward; it incorporates another year of growth in digital advertising revenue,” he said.

“So the total pool for media will be bigger by that year of growth.”

LinkedIn will no longer be exempt from Australian laws requiring global tech giants to pay for news content on their platforms, if it wants to avoid the increased taxes.

Google, Meta, TikTok and now the Microsoft-owned LinkedIn will all have to make deals with eight media organisations, or pay 2.5 per cent of their digital revenue generated in Australia.

The penalty levy is applied to eligible tech companies with $250 million or more in local digital advertising revenue.

canberra.title: Canberra is being invited to dinner and there’s one big question on the table
canberra.snippet: In an effort to find better dinner conversation, Gretel Van-Lane, founder of Wollongong-based Dinners with a Difference, has hosted more ...
canberra.content:
Gretel Van-Lane personally hosts Dinners With A Difference to facilitate good conversation. Photo: Dinners with a Difference.

In an effort to find better dinner conversation, Gretel Van-Lane, founder of Wollongong-based Dinners with a Difference, has hosted more than 1000 people at her dinner table, and now she wants to hear what Canberrans have to say by bringing the popular event to Bar Beirut at the end of the month.

The concept, which Gretel simply refers to as ‘Dinners’, is an opportunity for strangers to meet over a good meal and take part in a facilitated conversation hosted by Gretel.

“I ran women’s circles for many years, and I love that because you get great depth and breadth in conversations, but I wanted to hear more people’s perspectives, people who may not come to a women’s circle, and I wanted to include food and wine because I like that too,” laughs Gretel.

The popular Wollongong event has seen more than 1000 diners engage in good conversation. Photo: Dinners with a Difference.

With the sell-out events bringing together hundreds of diners over four years, you might think the conversations could get a bit dry, but Gretel has worked out the secret to focused and full conversations. She arms attendees with a topic, preps them for the rules of engagement in advance and personally hosts the room to ensure everyone has a chance to share their ideas in a safe and convivial environment. For her first Canberra event, Gretel is bringing along the topic A Good Life, and it’s one that Gretel says always sparks hearty conversation.

“It’s the fourth time I’ll be hosting this topic, and I’ve found over the years that the way people broach it has evolved, it gives people a moment to stop and reflect, and who doesn’t want to live a good life?”

With people from all walks of life joining her at the table, Gretel is continually amazed by her guests.

“It takes a really generous person that comes along and goes, ‘Yeah, tell me about your life story. I’m really interested, and I actually want to share mine.'”

Well known for a love of food and life, Gretel has chosen the perfect venue in Bar Beirut for her first Canberra event. Photo: Ben Calvert.

You don’t have to talk to Gretel for long to see why she’d make a great host. Every word is thoughtful; her mind is continually full of wonder and curiosity, and it’s an approach she took into finding the right venue when she landed on a Canberra favourite, Bar Beirut.

“What really struck me was not only Bar Beirut’s love of food but their love for community and the importance of belonging,” shares Gretel.

The loneliness epidemic is one of Gretel’s great motivators for continuing the event despite working a busy day job, and while couples and friends do attend, she shares that many of her guests come alone.

“I think it takes real courage to turn away from our phone, get out of the house, and try something new. And I feel like Dinners is one of those places that people can come and be social which is unlike anything else. There aren’t many places you can go by yourself and leave feeling more connected.”

The Canberra edition of Dinners With A Difference will be held on Thursday 20 August at Bar Beirut. Tickets are available on Humantix.

australia.title: Pocock and crossbenchers call Labor’s NDIS overhaul ‘too far, too fast’ in scathing Senate inquiry report
australia.snippet: Greens say Labor’s reform set to ‘rip life-changing supports away from disabled people instead of raising additional revenue through taxi...
australia.content:
Cross-benchers have slammed the Albanese government’s proposed overhaul of the NDIS as going “too far, too fast” as the changes to curb the growth of the $52bn program appear set to pass the parliament as early as next week.

The Greens and independent ACT senator, David Pocock, delivered scathing assessments of the bill they warn will enable blunt and indiscriminate cuts to individual budgets supporting more than 770,000 Australians with disabilities in a final Senate inquiry report released on Friday afternoon.

While the Labor-chaired committee recommended the bill pass, Greens senator Jordon Steele-John said the proposals would be “devastating to the lives of disabled people and their families”.

The bill forms part of the government’s plan to get the NDIS “back on track” and save $37.8bn over four years by tightening the eligibility criteria and subjecting all participants to independent functional assessments from 2028.

It will also give the NDIS minister, Mark Butler, the power to reduce funding categories for individuals by up to 99%. The government has already said it will apply a 50% reduction in individual participant budgets for social, civic and community participation.

Without the interventions, the government estimates the $52bn-a-year scheme will more than double in cost to $117bn a year in a decade’s time.

The Greens have acknowledged some changes should be made to make the NDIS work better for participants but suggested the scheme could be funded by a gas export tax.

“The choice that this Labor government is making is to rip life-changing supports away from disabled people instead of raising additional revenue through taxing gas exports shows their priorities clearly,” Steele-John wrote.

“This government is choosing the profits of large corporations over the lives of disabled people.”

Guardian Australia has previously reported that 241,000 NDIS participants will be shifted off the scheme by June 2031 after the introduction of the functional capacity test, to keep the number of participants at about 600,000.

During that period, an additional 105,000 will be stopped from entering the scheme.

Those shifted from the scheme are expected to be supported by programs run by states and territories with joint funding from the Commonwealth.

Pocock said no participant should be removed from the NDIS until those new programs are “funded, operating and accessible”, vowing to continue scrutiny of the changes.

“The true measure of these changes will be found in the experiences of people with disability. They must remain at the centre of what comes next,” Pocock said.

Coalition senators provided additional comments raising concerns that fraud and integrity within the NDIS had not been sufficiently addressed.

The government is expected to land a deal with the opposition early next week in order to pass the bill in the Senate.

Disability advocacy groups have been extremely critical of the government’s amendments to the NDIS, and have warned caring responsibilities will be shifted from the scheme to families, affecting women disproportionately.

Women With Disabilities Australia’s chief executive, Sophie Cusworth, said the government should deliver a comprehensive gender impact assessment of the bill.

“You cannot say you are working for women while looking to pass legislation that puts women’s safety, care, health and economic security at risk,” she said on Friday.

“That is not gender equality. That is neglect.”

australia.title: Lending to property investors falls sharply in ‘tiny’ step towards fairer housing market in Australia, expert says
australia.snippet: ABS data shows an almost 9% slump in new lending to investors after three interest rate hikes this year Follow our Australia news live bl...
australia.content:
In what one economist is describing as a “tiny step” toward a fairer housing market after decades of bad policy, property investors are shying away from established homes, and putting money into new builds instead, new data shows.

New lending to property investors fell sharply in the three months to June, slumping almost 9%, ABS data showed, while the number of total new home loans dropped by 5.4% in the June quarter.

The major banks have all reported a slump in mortgage applications in recent months, after three RBA official rate hikes and the federal budget’s investor tax changes that together have weighed on property prices.

The ABS’s head of finance statistics, Mish Tan, said: “lending fell across all borrower types this quarter and returned to similar levels to this time last year”.

Investor loans led the decline, falling by 8.6% in the June quarter after a 4.7% drop in the previous period. The number of investor loans was 2.8% higher than a year earlier, while the value of loans to investors was down by 10.2%.

The number of loans to first home buyers dropped by 2.9% over the three-month period, to be flat over the year.

Saul Eslake, a leading housing economist said the interest rates increases this year would be reducing the number of first home buyers..

“I don’t think it’s a cause for concern,” he said. “Whereas I would say the big fall in lending to investors for the purchase of established homes is actually something to be welcomed and celebrated.

“Because it means that prospective first home buyers are facing less competition from investors motivated by tax breaks for the housing we’ve already got.”

The number of loans to investors in established properties was down 14.8%, but the number of loans to investors buying new builds was up by 4.4% to a record high, a possible effect of the government’s budget carve-out for investor lending to build new housing.

Eslake said more investment in new builds actually increased rental supply, rather than pitting renters against investors for established housing.

He said these stats were a “tiny step” in the right direction to make Australia’s housing market more equal.

“A tiny step. But at least it is in that direction, whereas we’ve been taking tens of thousands of steps in the wrong direction for the last thirty years.”

National spokesperson for Everybody’s Home, Maiy Azize, said the figures show the governments tax reforms were “beginning to rebalance the market”.

“The most encouraging sign is that investors are pulling back from existing homes while investment in new housing is growing. That means less competition for first home buyers trying to buy a home,” Azize said.

“It also smashes the myth that immigration is the main driver of house prices. When governments change the rules and stop boosting investors, housing costs go down.

“Housing becoming more affordable is a good thing, especially for people trying to buy their first home.”

australia.title: Alleged victim says Alan Jones groped him at lunch and describes fear of being seen as broadcaster’s ‘toy’, court hears
australia.snippet: Former 2GB and 2UE radio broadcaster is facing 22 indecent assault and sexual touching charges. Jones, 85, has pleaded not guilty Follow ...
australia.content:
A young driver for Alan Jones felt “violated” and “trapped” when the broadcaster allegedly touched him on the penis in the car and kissed him in a lift, but didn’t complain due to the “extraordinary” power dynamic between the pair, a Sydney court has been told.

Complainant C, now aged in his 40s, on Friday told Jones’s indecent assault trial that interactions between the pair escalated over time.

C, who was 18 when he started working at 2GB in the mid-2000s, told Downing Centre local court the unwanted touching began a few years later, in the car and a lift at the radio host’s harbourside apartment.

Jones has pleaded not guilty to 20 charges of indecent assault and two counts of sexual touching against six complainants.

The alleged victim told the court he felt “deeply, deeply embarrassed” when colleagues said they saw Jones groping his penis under the table at a function in Mosman.

C said Jones instructed him to sit next to him and spent the entire lunch with his left hand under the table and either on his leg or on his penis over his pants.

“[A colleague] was looking at me while Alan was touching my penis,” C said.

Prosecutor Georgina Wright asked: “Did [the colleague] have any look on his face?

C replied: “Yes it was a smirk.”

“I didn’t want them thinking I was Alan’s toy. I know that sounds like a simplistic way of putting it, but they all made jokes about Alan being interested in young men.”

Asked why he didn’t move his hand away, C said: “If I moved his hand it would draw attention to me and I didn’t want people to know what was happening”.

On the way back to the car after lunch the colleague, speaking in a joking tone, said to C: “You copped a feel under the table, did you like it?”

Asked how he felt by Wright, C said “deeply, deeply embarrassed”.

“That was the first time someone had seen him touch me,” C said.

Wright asked: “How did you react?”

C said: “My reaction was embarrassment. I don’t recall what I said because I was really, really, really embarrassed.”

“I probably tried to laugh it off.”

The young man said he aspired to be a producer but was required to make the 2GB host’s breakfast of soft-boiled eggs with bread soldiers, clean his bathroom at the radio station and iron underpants.

He was “star-struck” when the broadcaster offered to pay him $40,000 a year to be his driver, C told the court.

“Alan had a kitchen in his office and I had to make soft-boiled eggs and Burgen bread … and cut it into soldiers,” C said. “I took it in on a tray and had a cloth napkin on my arm.”

C said he had to loiter around the studio waiting for an opportunity to go in because if he left the empty tray too long he was berated by the broadcaster.

“It was pretty aggressive; ‘get this out of here’ sort of thing,” C said when questioned by Wright.

Complainant C, the second alleged victim to give evidence at the trial, told the court he grew up listening to talkback radio and all he ever wanted to do was work at a radio station. But, C said, he did not want to be a chauffeur or a butler.

After the show ended each day, he drove Jones home, the court was told. C wanted to go back and work at the radio station but was often required to complete household tasks under the direction of Jones’s butler.

He said he was given the smaller items to iron, including handkerchiefs and underpants. “If I stuffed it up it wouldn’t have been the end of the world,” C said.

He was given a foot in the door by fellow shock jock Ray Hadley, who paid him for three months out of his own pocket before he secured full-time employment.

Complainant C didn’t sign a contract because Jones told him contracts tended to “intimidate young people”, he told the court.

“I just wanted to work in radio,” C said. “It was a dream to work at that radio station, and to be able to say I worked with Alan Jones was as good as it gets for a young kid who wants to work in radio.”

Complainant C said the first time the broadcaster touched his penis while he was driving him home, C felt Jones’s hand go from his knee, up to his left leg and over his penis on the outside his pants.

The former driver said he froze and when Jones got out of the car he felt “violated”.

“I never had a man touch me on the penis before,” C told the court on Friday. “I’m not gay.”

C said he didn’t report the touching at the time because he was scared. Similar incidents occurred for weeks before Jones tried to kiss him, the complainant said.

The first time Jones allegedly kissed him, C had parked Jones’s car underneath his apartment building and was carrying the broadcaster’s jacket in his left hand, and his briefcase in his right.

The two entered the lift, and C walked to the back as Jones came towards him, the court heard.

Jones’s face encroached on C’s, but with his hands full, the driver could only drop his head, putting his chin to his neck in an attempt to avoid his employer, the witness said.

C re-enacted the motion in court, shaking his head and saying “no, no, no, no” repeatedly.

“I didn’t want him to kiss me,” C said on Friday before crying.

Jones allegedly did the same on two more occasions, putting his hand on C’s face in a “romantic” way before kissing him on the lips.

“I didn’t kiss him back,” C told the court. “A kiss is two people kissing each other, and I never leant forward. I closed my mouth as tight as possible and just dealt with it.”

C said he would try to drop Jones off in front of his apartment so he could avoid the elevator.

“If I was lucky, he’d get out, if I wasn’t, he’d point to the underground car park,” the complainant said.

In the lift, with his hands full, C said: “I felt trapped.”

“The power dynamic was extraordinary,” C told the court. “This bloke was my boss, he owned the radio station, I couldn’t say no.”

The trial before judge Glenn Walsh continues.

australia.title: Teachers demand more scrutiny of Catholic school funding amid allegations of ‘sham arrangement’ with NSW Liberal group
australia.snippet: Independent Education Union ‘deeply concerned … public funding for Catholic schools may have been wrongfully spent on Liberal party matte...
australia.content:
The union for independent school teachers in New South Wales has demanded greater scrutiny of Catholic schools as the chief executive of their governing body told a corruption inquiry payments to a lobbying firm were not a “sham arrangement” to fund Liberal party factional work.

Dallas McInerney insisted to the NSW Independent Commission Against Corruption (Icac) on Friday that Catholic Schools NSW funding wasn’t misused.

Icac is investigating whether McInerney arranged and approved illegal donations from the governing body for 600 Catholic schools to support alleged branch stacking efforts of the Christian factional group the Reformers.

The group wanted more conservative policies on issues such as abortion, euthanasia and same-sex marriage.

The inquiry has heard that Catholic Schools NSW paid Beckington, a lobbying company run by Reformers Christian Ellis and Jeremy Greenwood, $130,900 through invoices for consulting services between August 2019 and August 2021.

Greenwood’s company, JPG Advisory, was paid $135,000 between December 2021 and December 2023. The commission has heard that Reformers Robert Assaf and Dylan Whitelaw spent work hours on factional efforts while employed at Catholic Schools NSW.

On Friday, the Independent Education Union’s NSW branch, which had previously declined to comment while the inquiry was under way, said it was “deeply concerned by … [allegations] that public funding for Catholic schools may have been wrongfully spent on Liberal party matters”.

The IEU NSW/ACT branch secretary, Carol Matthews, said close scrutiny of public funding “was not applied to organisations such as Catholic Schools NSW that receive funding on behalf of Catholic diocesan schools”.

“Regardless of the findings of Icac in this matter, there should be greater scrutiny of bodies such as Catholic Schools NSW, which receive public funding on behalf of non-government schools,” Matthews said in a statement.

About 80% of the funding distributed by Catholic Schools NSW comes from the state and federal governments. Government funding totalled about $3.8bn in 2024. The NSW premier, Chris Minns, has ruled out an independent audit of the schools governing body while Icac’s inquiry is under way.

McInerney stood aside from his role as CEO before the Icac hearings began “to allow the work of Catholic Schools NSW to continue its important mission”, he said in a statement previously. Catholic Schools NSW has previously said it “does not intend … to provide responses to questions that supersede the eight-week inquiry and legal process that is under way”.

McInerney on Friday was asked about messages in February 2021 between Assaf and fellow Reformer Jean-Claude Perrottet, the younger brother of former NSW premier Dominic Perrottet, who is not accused of wrongdoing. Assaf and Jean-Claude were not directly employed by Beckington.

Jean-Claude Perrottet wrote to Assaf: “Ellis and I caught up with Dallas in Bowral to discuss money, had a long convo.”

The counsel assisting Juliet Curtin asked if the reason for Assaf and Jean-Claude’s interest was “because they knew that the arrangement in place was that you would pay Beckington money pursuant to a sham arrangement” – under which the money would come to them.

“No,” McInerney said on Friday. He said he could not recall the Bowral meeting. McInerney rejected evidence previously given by Assaf to the inquiry that Greenwood and McInerney met this year to discuss their summons.

The inquiry has previously heard that Jean-Claude Perrottet received money from Beckington. When the Catholic Schools NSW contract moved in 2021 from Beckington to JPG Advisory, Assaf and Jean-Claude allegedly each received a “kickback”, in Jean-Claude’s case, 50% of the monthly retainer, after he secured the contract with McInerney.

On Friday, McInerney repeatedly described Jean-Claude Perrottet as his “conduit” to Greenwood, who ran JPG.

Dylan Whitelaw, who worked at Beckington after being employed by McInerney at Catholic Schools NSW, has previously given evidence there was an arrangement under which payments from the schools’ governing body to Beckington were used to fund Reformers’ activities. McInerney repeatedly denied this.

McInerney was asked on Friday why Whitelaw, then only 21, was involved in negotiating an increase in Beckington’s retainer in 2021, and why McInerney cited Whitelaw’s departure from the company as a reason to end the contract with Beckington.

“I’m not confident they’ll have the in-house expertise to support our needs in the way DW [Dylan Whitelaw] has been,” McInerney wrote to a colleague.

On Friday, McInerney, who described Whitelaw as a “junior” at Beckington who carried out an “account manager” role and was responsible for “administrative interplay”, said his language had been consistent.

“Your in-house expertise as an account manager is … knowing the client, the rhythms, the relationships, how they service,” he said. The inquiry has previously heard that McInerney came to know Whitelaw through the Mittagoing Liberal branch after first meeting his parents. He employed Whitelaw at Catholic Schools NSW in 2019 after he graduated high school.

On Thursday, McInerney said correspondence leading up to the Beckington contract in which he told Ellis to get an ABN and a mailbox was “traditional due diligence”. He denied he was attempting to provide “a veneer of legitimacy” to the contract.

On Friday, the inquiry – and McInerney – learned that the ABN provided by Ellis in fact belonged to Ellis’s sister.

After Curtin suggested it showed due diligence “wasn’t particularly effective”, McInerney said: “I will add the point [that] I thought it was, but I’m happy to be enlightened”. The inquiry heard Beckington later wrote Catholic Schools NSW’s name incorrectly on invoices.

After Curtin suggested evidence of written work by Beckington was “de minimis”, apart from calendar entries for monthly meetings, McInerney insisted Beckington did consult for Catholic Schools NSW.

Asked if Beckington’s input was “only ever given orally”, McInerney said that Beckington had contributed to two “forward plans for public affairs and engagement in 2019” which involved “exhaustive planning sessions”.

The commission heard McInerney provided the two documents but there was no written evidence of Beckington being involved in the drafting process.

McInerney was expected to appear again before Icac next week.

australia.title: Bet365 apologises after children wear gambling logos in charity race – as it happened
australia.snippet: This blog has now closed Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Albanese says gambling inducements are ‘over the to...
australia.content:
Bet365 apologises to senate after children wear gambling logos in charity race

Henry Belot

Global gambling giant Bet365 has apologised to the senate after children were dressed in its branded clothing during a fundraising event at a local racecourse.

In April, the children were invited to take part in a running relay at Terang Racing Club. The winning team would receive $1000 from Bet365, which would be donated to a local sports club.

Footage of the event was broadcast on the Racing.com website. The footage shows children wearing racing bibs and caps with the Bet365 logo while taking part in the race.

At one point in the broadcast, the host is heard saying: “I look over (at one team) and the average age I reckon is about 13 or 14. What’s going on there?”

One parent at the racecourse objected to children being draped in clothing from the gambling industry and complained to ACT independent senator, David Pocock, who raised the matter with Bet365 during a parliamentary inquiry.

In a response tabled to the inquiry, Bet365 said it had not been aware of its clothing being distributed to children and would never have allowed this to happen:

Bet365 is sorry that this happened and would like the community to know that it has never and will never authorise or cause minors to wear Bet365 clothing or marketing.

Bet365 takes its legal and regulatory responsibilities very seriously and was shocked and embarrassed to learn that its branding had been used in this way.

Bet365 said the decision to dress the children in its clothes was taken by volunteers from the Terang Racing Club. The club has been contacted for comment.

  • 14h ago

    Welcome

What we learned, Friday 14 August

That’s another day of our live coverage done!

Before we go, let’s recap the day’s top headlines:

  • KPMG has contacted the man who blew the whistle on its audit leaks scandal to apologise ahead of an inquiry into its failures today.

  • Anthony Albanese and the US president, Donald Trump, spoke overnight, with the prime minister saying they had a “productive” and “substantial” call about a “number of global and regional issues”.

  • Parents of children who took their own lives and who campaigned for the under 16s social media ban prior to its introduction have rejected claims the ban is not working or has failed, as they call for the government to increase the fines for non-compliance beyond the planned $99m level.

  • Qantas has refunded hundreds of customers aboard an A380 jet that was delayed for days after mechanical issues stranded passengers in Johannesburg, South Africa, for two nights.

  • Johnny Young, the singer-songwriter and producer who created and hosted the popular variety show Young Talent Time, has died aged 79.

  • The organisation that manages Australian skies has defended its decision not to immediately report a fresh safety incident at Sydney airport when a Virgin plane aborted its takeoff.

  • Victoria’s recently deposed Labor premier, Jacinta Allan, has announced she will leave politics at the next election.

  • The shadow housing minister, Andrew Bragg, did not mean to suggest he supported substandard houses being built as part of his proposal to reduce nearly 2,000 pages of building standard requirements to 80 pages.

  • Former CFMEU boss John Setka has been charged by Victorian police after an investigation into allegedly threatening and harassing emails sent to union administrators.

Thanks for joining us, have a lovely weekend!

Luca Ittimani

KPMG deputy chief lawyer’s voice breaks as he claims colleagues ‘misleading if not deceptive’

KPMG’s top lawyer’s deputy has delivered emotional evidence to a parliamentary committee, saying his colleagues misled him when he tried to investigate leak allegations.

James McLelland, the firm’s deputy counsel, said he carried out an initial investigation on the instruction of the former chief executive Andrew Yates in late December 2024 and updated in June 2025.

The inquiry has heard excerpts from his investigation today. McLelland said:

I’m of the view that the work that I undertook was fundamentally undermined by the answers that were given, which were misleading if not directly deceptive, to the questions that I asked; and undermined by limitations in scope …

I’ve never had an opportunity to meet the whistleblower. I want to take the opportunity to say I am sorry. I am sorry I have been part of this.

His voice broke and he appeared to grow emotional as he spoke. The committee chair, Deb O’Neill, encouraged him to have a glass of water. She said:

There is a clarion sound of truth in what you’ve put on the record there.

McLelland described his reaction to reading the report written from his investigation for the first time yesterday:

I was angry, frustrated and hugely disappointed that that had occurred … The entire engagement and sequence of events for the firm would have been fundamentally different if those individuals, to my mind, had answered those questions honestly.

Partners at law firm Allens earlier today gave evidence that their own investigation found evidence contradicting the testimony of KPMG partners Eileen Hoggett, Paul Rogers and Kim Lawry.

Bet365 apologises to senate after children wear gambling logos in charity race

Henry Belot

Global gambling giant Bet365 has apologised to the senate after children were dressed in its branded clothing during a fundraising event at a local racecourse.

In April, the children were invited to take part in a running relay at Terang Racing Club. The winning team would receive $1000 from Bet365, which would be donated to a local sports club.

Footage of the event was broadcast on the Racing.com website. The footage shows children wearing racing bibs and caps with the Bet365 logo while taking part in the race.

At one point in the broadcast, the host is heard saying: “I look over (at one team) and the average age I reckon is about 13 or 14. What’s going on there?”

One parent at the racecourse objected to children being draped in clothing from the gambling industry and complained to ACT independent senator, David Pocock, who raised the matter with Bet365 during a parliamentary inquiry.

In a response tabled to the inquiry, Bet365 said it had not been aware of its clothing being distributed to children and would never have allowed this to happen:

Bet365 is sorry that this happened and would like the community to know that it has never and will never authorise or cause minors to wear Bet365 clothing or marketing.

Bet365 takes its legal and regulatory responsibilities very seriously and was shocked and embarrassed to learn that its branding had been used in this way.

Bet365 said the decision to dress the children in its clothes was taken by volunteers from the Terang Racing Club. The club has been contacted for comment.

Search for missing NSW 18-year-old bushwalker enters second day

The search for a missing 18-year-old woman in Nattai national park in the Southern Highlands has entered its second day.

Lily Hooper was last seen leaving a home on Burragorang Road in Oakdale at about 8am on Wednesday morning to go hiking.

Her family has been unable to locate or contact her since and holds “serious concerns for her welfare”.

Her car was found near the Bonnum Pic Walking Trail in the national park.

Emergency services, including police, ambulance and Fire and Rescue NSW, continue to conduct air and land searches.

Penry Buckley

Teachers union calls for greater scrutiny of Catholic schools amid Icac allegations

The union for independent schools teachers in NSW has called for greater scrutiny by the state government of independent Catholic schools, amid Icac allegations public funding may have been used for factional Liberal party work.

Dallas McInerney, the CEO of Catholic Schools NSW, the governing body for more than 600 schools in the state, has finished giving evidence to Icac’s inquiry into allegations of corruption in the NSW Liberal party. He is expected to return on Wednesday.

During the inquiry, the commission has heard from members of conservative Christian Liberal group the Reformers employed by Catholic Schools NSW that they spent working hours on factional efforts. McInerney repeatedly denied payments totalling $265,900 by Catholic Schools NSW to two registered lobbying companies controlled by the Reformers were really to fund branch stacking efforts.

About 80% of the funding distributed by Catholic Schools NSW comes from the state and federal governments, or about $3.8bn in 2024. In a statement today, the NSW/ACT Independent Education Union (IEU) said it was “deeply concerned by … [allegations] that public funding for Catholic schools may have been wrongfully spent on Liberal party matters”. Branch secretary Carol Matthews said:

Responsible school expenditure includes professional learning for school staff, development of curriculum materials, support for students with disabilities, and adequate pay and working conditions for staff who deliver quality education … However, similar scrutiny is not applied to organisations such as Catholic Schools NSW that receive funding on behalf of Catholic diocesan schools.

Regardless of the findings of Icac in this matter, there should be greater scrutiny of bodies such as Catholic Schools NSW, which receive public funding on behalf of non-government schools.

The NSW premier, Chris Minns, has ruled out an independent audit of the schools governing body while Icac’s inquiry is under way. McInerney stood aside from his role as CEO before hearings began, “to allow the work of Catholic Schools NSW to continue its important mission”. Catholic Schools NSW has declined to comment on issues arising from the inquiry before it concludes.

Former CFMEU boss John Setka charged for alleged threats to union administrators

Nino Bucci

Former CFMEU boss John Setka has been charged by Victorian police after an investigation into allegedly threatening and harassing emails sent to union administrators.

Police said in a statement that a 61-year-old man from Footscray was arrested on Friday morning. Police said:

He has since been charged with using a telecom communications device to menace, using a telecom communications device to offend and two charges of commit indictable offence while on bail.

The man will appear at Melbourne magistrates court later today.

Police will allege harassing and offensive comments were made online on Monday (10 August).

Setka was arrested in November last year and charged with seven counts of using a telecommunications device to menace, harass, and offend.

He was further charged on 25 February with using a carriage service to harass and committing an indictable offence while on bail.

Police will allege additional threats were made and an IVO was served on the man in July.

Setka was charged by officers from taskforce Hawk, which targets criminal behaviour linked to the construction industry.

He resigned as CFMEU secretary in July 2024.

Nick Visser

That’s all from me. Achol Arok will take it from here and round out the week. Take care.

Patrick Commins

Liberals declare undying support for WA GST deal

Michaelia Cash, the Liberal senator for Western Australia, says “over our dead bodies will they take a cent” from her home state, after a Productivity Commission report slammed the Morrison-era deal that has funnelled tens of billions of extra taxpayer dollars to WA.

The prime minister and treasurer have already flagged they have no intention of altering the vote-winning arrangements, which the PC recommended should be reversed.

But Cash, in a statement alongside fellow West Australian Andrew Hastie, MP, said “Anthony Albanese has proved time and again that his word can’t be trusted so anything he says in regard to WA’s GST share should be taken with a grain of salt”.

He lied to Australians about capital gains tax and negative gearing and explained it away as changing his position. There’s no doubt he will change his position on WA’s GST as well.

Hastie said:

Anthony Albanese and Jim Chalmers have repeatedly promised Western Australians they would protect this deal. We will hold them to that promise between now and the final report in December.

Patrick Commins

Chalmers says WA must get its ‘fair share’ of GST

Jim Chalmers says Western Australia “must always get its fair share” of the $100bn GST pool, after the Productivity Commission in an interim report slammed the 2018 Morrison-era deal with WA as a multi-billion-dollar mistake that has only benefited the country’s richest state.

The treasurer made the comments in a statement after a meeting with his state and territory counterparts, where the government committed $460m as an incentive for states to streamline interstate rules around heavy trucking and health care providers such as nurses.

Danielle Wood, the PC’s chair, briefed the treasurers’ meeting on its GST interim report, which argues the WA deal should be unwound.

Chalmers said:

The Productivity Commission’s final report will be released later this year. Without pre-empting that report, the Albanese government has been clear that Western Australia must always get its fair share.

Roger Cook, WA’s premier, in a statement said “an attack on WA’s GST deal is an attack on all Western Australians”.

“Western Australia is the economic powerhouse of the nation. When WA does well, so does Australia,” Cook said, echoing comments from prime minister Anthony Albanese earlier today.

Shadow housing minister ‘misheard’ question over whether low-income Australians should accept substandard houses

Sarah Basford Canales

The shadow housing minister, Andrew Bragg, did not mean to suggest he supported substandard houses being built as part of his proposal to reduce nearly 2,000 pages of building standard requirements to 80 pages.

The NSW senator wrote on social media he had misheard the question, adding “houses built to this standard would be strong, safe and sound homes with all the basic amenity, such as insulation, plumbing, sewerage etc”.

I did not intend to agree that houses complying with the Basic Australian Standard would be ‘substandard’. They wouldn’t be.

Bragg’s address to the National Press Club this week proposed condensing the National Construction Code from nearly 2,000 pages to just 80 in an effort to get more “basic and safe” homes built by doing away with “optional extras” such as compulsory energy efficiency and accessibility measures.

Yesterday, Bragg was asked on ABC Radio National whether this meant low-income earners should accept substandard housing. He replied “yes, definitely”.

Amanda Meade

Back to the Alan Jones trial

Alan Jones’s alleged victim became emotional in the witness box as he recounted how his boss allegedly kissed him in the lift for the first time after a drive from work to his harbourside apartment.

Complainant C told Downing Centre local court that when the lift doors from the parking garage under the apartment shut, “Alan came towards me and I thought he’s trying to kiss me here”.

“I remember dropping my head, making it inaccessible to kiss me and you’re trying to stop someone … I didn’t know what to do,” C told the indecent assault trial in Sydney.

Jones has pleaded not guilty to 20 indecent assault charges and two sexual touching charges in relation to six men.

Complainant C told the court today he dropped his head and moved it from side to side to avoid Jones’s kiss.

“It was a pretty tight space, he turned and faced me and advanced towards me,” C said.

C was crying and hung his head as he detailed how Jones allegedly kissed him for the first time.

“I didn’t want him to kiss me,” he told the court.

Judge Glenn Walsh asked C if he wanted a break but C said he was OK.

Jones walked out of the lift into his apartment after kissing C, the court heard.

The witness said Jones would often hold his face in a romantic way when he kissed him, but C never kissed the broadcaster back.

Asked if he consented to Jones kissing him on the lips and touching him on the face and the arm, he said no.

KPMG paid $500,000 to second whistleblower as more step forward, inquiry hears

Luca Ittimani

More whistleblowers have come forward to raise concerns about KPMG, a parliamentary inquiry has heard.

The inquiry started after a whistleblower flagged audit team leaks.

Senator Barbara Pocock has asked about another case of KPMG “silencing a whistleblower in an attempt to deal with allegations of wrongdoing by the firm,” this time in its tax division, as first reported by the Australian Financial Review.

KPMG’s former chair, Martin Sheppard, told the inquiry the claim was settled in late 2024, likely with a payment of about $500,000. He said there would have been a confidential deed of settlement, likely with non-disparagement provisions, but with no restrictions on further lawsuits or claims against other parties.

KPMG’s former chief executive, Andrew Yates, said the allegations mostly dated back 25 years. He said the whistleblower “was reluctant to provide information directly to the firm” so they shared information with law firm Allens instead. Yates said:

We did try and investigate but the passage of time had been so long that we were just unable to find information.

Pocock asked the firm to detail any other settlement agreements of this nature over the last decade, and explain why they were made and how much the firm paid out to settle issues.

Senator Deborah O’Neill later added:

There are many many more who are contacting us and they are talking about a repeat of the same behaviour.

Patrick Commins

New home loans fall in June quarter: ABS

New lending to property investors fell sharply in the three months to June, according to ABS figures, which also showed a retreat in loans to first home buyers.

The major banks over recent days have all reported a slump in mortgage applications during the June quarter, in the wake of three RBA rate hikes and the budget’s investor tax changes that together have weighed on property prices.

The Australian Bureau of Statistics data show the number of total new home loans dropped by 5.4% over the three-month period.

Mish Tan, the ABS’s head of finance statistics, said “lending fell across all borrower types this quarter and returned to similar levels to this time last year”.

Investor loans led the decline, falling by 8.6% in the June quarter after a 4.7% drop in the previous period. The number of investor loans was 2.8% higher than a year earlier.

But in an early vindication of the government’s budget carve-out for investor lending to build new homes, loans in this category rose 4.4% in the quarter.

However, the number of loans to first home buyers dropped by 2.9% over the three-month period, to be flat over the year.

The number of new owner-occupier loans in total fell 3.3% in the June quarter and were 1.6% down on a year earlier – the first annual fall since September 2023, the ABS said.

Nick Miller

Where is Australia’s Count Binface?

We’re all waiting eagerly for the result in the UK’s Clacton byelection, where Reform leader Nigel Farage faces a record field of challengers (including an alien dressed as a bin and two Australians).

As the votes are counted veteran psephologist Antony Green found himself wondering: “why are there no Count Binfaces in Australia?”.

In a blog post this morning, he explains:

It sort of used to occur, but the law was tightened after several protest candidates representing the Abolish Child Support/Family Court Party adopted vvvveeerrrryyyy lloonngg names to contest the 1998 Federal election.

This included a candidate who appeared on the ballot paper as “Prime Minister John Piss The Family Court and Legal Aid” in John Howard’s seat of Bennelong.

Now candidates must use their names, or shortened versions, that appear on the electoral roll – much to the disappointment of “Brisbane performer Tamara Tonite [who was] complaining that her electoral enrolment change form had been rejected under her known-as drag name,” Green wrote.

One did slip through, though:

Ahead of the 2007 Federal election, some junior clerk doing enrolments allowed a Mr “Of The Above None” to register, allowing him to appear on the ballot paper in the seat of Gilmore at the 2007 election as “NONE, Of The Above”.

Amanda Meade

Complainant tells court about first time Alan Jones allegedly touched him on the penis

Back in court, the judge has been told that the first time Alan Jones allegedly touched complainant C on the penis, C was driving the broadcaster from 2GB to his Circular Quay home and he felt “violated”.

“I’ve never had a man touch me on the penis before,” he said. “I am not gay.”

Sometimes Jones would touch it and sometimes he would rub it, C told the court, “moving up and down on the outside of my penis”.

After two weeks of reaching across and touching his leg in the car while he was driving, Jones progressed to regularly touching his penis, C said in court.

“It was not dissimilar to when he was touching my leg, it was any day he wasn’t on the phone or asleep, but if he was awake and alert it was more than likely he was going to touch me.”

The prosecutor Georgina Wright asked: “Why didn’t you say anything?”

C told the court: “I was scared. My boss’s hand was on my penis. If I told him stop, I don’t know what would have happened. You had to cop it.”

Complainant C became visibly emotional as he was giving his evidence. The trial continues.

Luca Ittimani

Sacked KPMG partner tells inquiry she doesn’t recall printing confidential info

The KPMG partner who was sacked for her role in the leaks scandal is asking the firm why it expelled her, saying she does not remember printing confidential documents.

Eileen Hoggett has been fined by KPMG, barred from practice by the accountants peak body and is being investigated by the regulator. She has told a parliamentary committee she did not recall printing or storing Lendlease’s confidential documents, a key allegation, adding:

I’m not here to defend or minimise the fact that the documents were printed and put in my locker but I am not aware that the documents were distributed widely or used to win new work.

Hoggett’s passive phrasing that they “were printed” drew further questioning, where she admitted she was the only person with access to her locker other than her personal assistant. She said her PA would only let others access her locker with her authority.

Senator Barbara Pocock read out a May 2023 email Hoggett sent to her personal assistant:

I think we confidentially allow him to look at the printed version in my locker when he’s back in Sydney. He needs to do it sensitively without letting too many people know.

Hoggett said the person mentioned is the director of the Lendlease document. KPMG has said this email was the reason Hoggett was expelled when it came to light in July.

Hoggett said the new chief executive, John Sams, rang her while she was out walking one morning, giving her “no opportunity to be heard or to have any discussion” about the expulsion. She said she didn’t understand why:

I did expect a different process ... that’s why I’m trying to ascertain from the firm the basis of my expulsion and to also understand my rights as a former partner.

Amanda Meade

Complainant tells court Alan Jones started ‘love bombing’ him with texts

In the Alan Jones trial, his former driver has told the court the broadcaster became very friendly and eventually started “love bombing him” with early-morning text messages such as: “Good morning darling … I hope you have a beautiful day, big hugs.”

“I would feel the need to respond in kind,” complainant C said.

C told the court that Jones started to talk about his penis in text messages, after C had said his own nickname should be “Donkey”.

“The messages were far more sexually explicit. It was like being bombarded, live love bombing,” he said.

C said one day Jones put his hand on his knee and squeezed it, and C gently tapped it away. It made him feel “uncomfortable”, the court heard.

Jones has denied 22 charges of indecent assault and sexual touching in relation to six alleged victims. The trial before judge Glenn Walsh continues.

world.title: American missionary kidnapped in Niger freed after nine months
world.snippet: Kevin Rideout, who was abducted by unknown assailants in Niamey, said to be in good health and in care of US officials An American missio...
world.content:
An American missionary who was kidnapped in Niger in October has been released, his organisation has said.

Kevin Rideout “is in good health in the care of US officials” and would soon be reunited with his extended family, SIM International said in a statement.

Rideout was kidnapped in the west African country’s capital, Niamey, on 21 October by three armed individuals and was probably driven out of town, according to a security official at the time. No armed group claimed responsibility for the abduction.

Niger has long been the target of attacks by armed groups, including jihadis linked to al-Qaida and Islamic State.

The US embassy in Niamey issued a security alert a day after Rideout’s abduction, warning that American citizens “remain at a heightened risk of kidnapping throughout Niger, including in the capital city”.

Niger is ruled by a military junta that took power in 2023 after deposing the democratically elected president, Mohamed Bazoum. The new authorities ousted western partners, including the US, which had soldiers in Niger, and forged a new security and diplomatic alliance with Russia.

In June, more than 30 people were killed when gunmen attacked the main airport in Niamey. It was the second attack this year at the airport, a strategic hub that serves as the ruling military’s command, hosting its air force base and most of its drones and aircraft. It is also the headquarters of the regional alliance that brings together troops from Niger, Mali and Burkina Faso.

The violence is the latest sign of armed groups increasingly targeting cities and urban centres in Africa’s Sahel region.

world.title: DRC’s fast-growing Ebola outbreak spreads to sixth province
world.snippet: Man dies in Bas-Uele after travelling from Haut-Uele, as head of WHO says outbreak on track to be deadliest ever The Ebola outbreak in th...
world.content:
The Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has spread to a sixth province, officials have said, a day after the head of the World Health Organization said the outbreak was on track to surpass the deadliest in history, which killed at least 11,000 people more than a decade ago.

The current outbreak has killed more than 2,100 people out of more than 4,500 cases, according to the latest government figures released on Tuesday. At the same point in the 2014-16 outbreak in west Africa, the previous most deadly outbreak, 755 cases had been recorded, according to WHO data.

Jean Kaseya, the director general of Africa CDC, said on Thursday that a death had been recorded in the previously unaffected Bas-Uele province. The man had travelled from Isiro, in Haut-Uele province, to Buta, the capital of Bas-Uele, where he died, Kaseya said.

There are no approved vaccines or treatments for the rare Bundibugyo strain of the virus that is responsible for the current outbreak.

The death toll has been reached almost three times faster than in the 2014-16 outbreak. On Wednesday, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, the WHO director general, said the current outbreak would surpass that one based on its current pace.

Six of DRC’s 26 provinces have now been affected, mainly those along the country’s north-eastern border. More than 3,400 of the cases have been recorded in Ituri province, where the outbreak was first reported.

Uganda has reported 20 cases, all in the capital, Kampala. The last case there was reported on 21 June and no community transmission has been recorded.

The DRC outbreak is unfolding amid strikes by some unpaid health workers, global development aid cuts, threats by rebel groups, anger from long-traumatised communities, and misinformation claiming that Ebola is not real.

Health workers at the Nizi treatment centre in Ituri province went on strike on Thursday, leading to the temporary closure of the centre, saying they had not been paid for three months.

The true scope of the outbreak remains unknown. It was declared on 15 May but the WHO says sequencing now shows it began months earlier in February.

Health authorities have said between 60% and 70% of new cases are recorded outside contacts being monitored, and that the disease is spreading at an alarming rate.

Dr Mohamed Yakub Janabi, the WHO regional director for Africa, said this week: “We are chasing the virus; the virus is ahead of us.”

Nonetheless, his colleague Abdirahman Mahamud, the head of the WHO’s emergency response division, sounded a note of optimism on Wednesday, saying that if the pandemic response was implemented “at the same time across the five transmission zones, we are expecting a turnaround in three months”.

Even with that, Mahamud said the peak of the outbreak would not be reached for six months under a “moderate” scenario and that the outbreak could last nine to 12 months.

Ebola is rare but highly contagious and can be contracted from body fluids such as vomit, blood or semen, including from dead bodies, and from contaminated surfaces and materials such as bedding and clothing. The disease it causes is severe and often fatal.

Clinical trials of two possible treatments for the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola causing this outbreak began last month in Ituri. Tedros said on Wednesday two vaccines developed specifically for this strain were now being tested on people for the first time.

This strain of Bundibugyo is genetically different from previous outbreaks in 2007 and 2012, making it likely that this outbreak began when the virus jumped from an infected animal to a human, researchers said in a paper published this week in the journal Nature Medicine. They had sequenced genomes from samples from 22 people with Ebola.

Last week, Kaseya said officials were worried the virus could be mutating and that the Africa CDC was planning further studies with the WHO to investigate.

Associated Press and Agence France-Presse contributed to this story.

world.title: French ambassador to CAR investigated over claims he hosted dozens of women
world.snippet: Disciplinary proceedings under way after security concerns raised over reported visits to official residence France has opened disciplina...
world.content:
France has opened disciplinary proceedings against its ambassador to Central African Republic over allegations of misconduct, after claims he brought dozens of women into his official residence, raising potential security concerns.

The investigation comes as Paris seeks to rebuild relations with CAR after their sharp deterioration in recent years amid Russia’s expanding influence in the former French colony.

The French weekly newspaper Le Canard enchaîné reported that the ambassador, Bruno Foucher, 65, brought about 30 women between the ages of 20 and 30 into his residence during the period of January 2024 to March 2026, with some of them staying overnight. The visits prompted officials to report a security breach.

The ambassador acknowledged having had sexual relations with two young women, the weekly said.

The French foreign ministry said: “At the initiative of the ministry, an administrative investigation was carried out in Bangui in 2026. Upon receipt of the findings of this mission, and at the request of the minister, the ministry initiated disciplinary proceedings against the ambassador. These proceedings are ongoing.”

The ministry conducted an on-site inspection in April, which led to the opening of disciplinary proceedings.

Foucher is a career diplomat who has served as ambassador to CAR since 2023. He was ambassador to Lebanon from 2017 to 2020, to Iran from 2011 to 2016, and to Chad between 2006 and 2011.

According to Le Canard enchaîné, which said it obtained the inspection report, the ambassador received about 15 visits a month.

He also allegedly instructed staff to allow one of the young women to stay at the residence during his absence.

Russia maintains a strong foothold in CAR, primarily through the Wagner paramilitary group, which plays a key role in providing security for the country’s president, Faustin-Archange Touadéra.

French officials have accused Russians of fostering anti-French sentiment in a number of African countries.

The French foreign minister, Jean-Noël Barrot, praised the “complete restoration of relations” between France and CAR when he visited Bangui in March.

world.title: Zambia elections haunted by ghost of incumbent president’s arch-rival
world.snippet: Hakainde Hichilema is bidding for second term, but feud between him and family of Edgar Lungu, who died in 2025, continues As Zambians go...
world.content:
As Zambians go to the polls on Thursday, the ghost of the current president’s predecessor hangs over the elections.

Hakainde Hichilema, 64, is bidding for a second term leading the southern African country after defeating his arch-rival Edgar Lungu by a landslide in 2021.

A feud between the two men, their families and supporters has dominated Zambian politics, to the extent that the quarrel has continued even after Lungu died in South Africa in June 2025.

Zambia’s government went to court to try to stop the burial of Lungu by his family, who did not want Hichilema presiding over a state funeral. In June, South Africa’s supreme court of appeal ruled in favour of Lungu’s family, overturning a previous high court decision in favour of the government.

In this election, Hichilema is facing the Tonse Alliance of opposition parties led by Brian Mundubile, 55, who was a government chief whip under Lungu. Mundubile’s running mate Makebi Zulu acted as the Lungu family’s spokesperson during the burial row, and on the campaign trail the two men have promised to bring Lungu’s body back to Zambia for a dignified burial.

The way death is dealt with is very important in Zambia, said Christopher Vandome, a senior research fellow at the thinktank Chatham House. “Even Hichilema supporters want to see due respect given to those that have died,” he said. “When it appears things get messy, it just makes the incumbent look disrespectful.”

The shadow of Lungu has also hung over allegations by the Tonse Alliance that Hichilema has deployed authoritarian tactics during the election campaign, including raiding its offices and detaining 36 members of Mundubile’s team.

Hichilema’s team furiously denied the claims, invoking Lungu’s treatment of Hichilema during the last election. “Zambians know what repression looks like. In 2021, the opposition leader [Hichilema] had been arrested 15 times, Prime TV [a private station] and the Post [a newspaper] had been shut down, and on election day the internet was switched off,” said a spokesperson for the ruling United Party for National Development. “Today the opposition campaigns freely across all 10 provinces, no media house has been closed and the airwaves are open.”

Transparency International Zambia monitors have recorded incidents of police interrupting opposition rallies, said Tamika Halwiindi, a coordinator at the organisation. “Disruptions from the police citing issues to do with safety have been noted to be more biased against the opposition and independents, as opposed to … the ruling party,” she said.

During Hichilema’s term, activists have also reported having peaceful demonstrations shut down. Mputa Ngalande of the Fight Inequality Alliance said he was among a group detained for more than 12 hours in July 2024 when they were protesting against the state power company during a period of 22-hour-a-day blackouts.

Vandome said: “[Hichilema’s] prospects of winning are very high. But his … personal lived experience of how complicated Zambian elections can be has given him this insecurity which is actually counting against him … denting his image in a way he doesn’t have to.”

Zambia’s economy has stabilised since an economic crisis, which was triggered when it defaulted on its debts in 2020 under Lungu. Annual inflation is now 6.5%, compared with 24.6% in July 2021. The government made primary and secondary education free in 2022.

Meanwhile, Zambia has attracted more international investment in recent years due to its huge deposits of copper, a key material in green technologies.

At the start of the month, in a giveaway to young voters, Hichilema, also known by his initials HH and nickname Bally (a slang word for an elder), told a crowd of jubilant university students that he was increasing their accommodation allowance by 50% with immediate effect.

However, the cost of living could still count against Hichilema in the elections, in which almost 8.8 million registered voters will also choose MPs and local councillors. The average annual income rose from $1,127 to $1,318 between 2021 and 2025, according to World Bank data. But prices almost doubled over the same period.

“What people are asking is: ‘If we are doing well economically, why are we not feeling impact on the ground?’” said Ngalende. “Because you will find on the ground that it is very difficult to access three meals a day.”

world.title: At least 44 dead after overcrowded ferry capsizes on Lake Kariba in Zimbabwe
world.snippet: Operation under way to rescue dozens missing after boat overturned by waves at world’s largest human-made lake At least 44 people have di...
world.content:
At least 44 people have died after an overcrowded ferry capsized on Lake Kariba in Zimbabwe, police said.

The boat had a capacity of 90 people, but was carrying 114 adult passengers, five crew members and an unknown number of children, Zimbabwe’s civil protection unit (CPU) said earlier on Wednesday, citing ticket sales.

A crew member told the national broadcaster ZBC that there were 153 people onboard when the ferry overturned on Tuesday after it hit large waves. A passenger told ZBC that the boat began taking on water about 30 minutes after it left the lakeshore town of Kariba, heading for islands and fishing camps.

A specialised underwater team was flown to the area, the CPU said, as search and rescue continued on Wednesday. At the time, the CPU said the death toll was 15, with 27 known to be missing.

Zimbabwe’s police updated the death toll on Wednesday afternoon in posts on X twice in the space of 32 minutes. In the first post, it said the death toll was 38, adding: “The bodies have been retrieved from the lake.” Then it said that 44 people were now known to have died.

A video shared by ZBC on Tuesday showed several people appearing to be sitting on the upturned ferry, while at least four speedboats came to their aid and a helicopter circled overhead.

Maxwell Kanhema Page, who describes himself as a media practitioner and originally posted the video shared by ZBC, reshared a video on his Facebook page filmed from the shore, in which he had noted that the lake was “angry”.

He said: “A few moments later I get over 200 calls about [the ferry] sinking. A sad day indeed.”

Lake Kariba is the world’s largest human-made lake by volume, stretching about 150 miles along Zimbabwe’s northern border with Zambia. It was created in the 1950s during British colonial rule, when the Zambezi River was dammed, displacing about 57,000 people. The Kariba dam supplies at least a third of both countries’ electricity.

It is not uncommon for boats to overturn on the lake. In 2014, 26 people, 24 of them children, drowned in Zambia’s part of the lake, when the boat meant to transport them to independence day celebrations capsized.

On the Zimbabwean side, five drowned in a 2021 incident and three were feared dead in an October 2023 capsizing. The month before, a police boat overturned although no one died.

Agence France-Presse contributed to this report.
